answer: $29 = 2^2 + 5^2$: a $\sqrt{29}$ square sits inside a $7\times7$ upright square with corners splitting its sides into $2$ and $5$, in two orientations; each of the $9$ upright $7\times7$ squares gives $2$.

solutions.title: Inscribe in a 7 by 7 square
solutions.body:
There are $3 \times 3 = 9$ upright $7 \times 7$ squares (the left side can be at $3$ positions, and likewise the bottom).

A tilted square with side $\sqrt{29}$ has its sides along vectors like $(2, 5)$ and $(-5, 2)$ since $29 = 2^2 + 5^2$ is the only way to write $29$ as a sum of two squares. So its bounding upright square has side $2 + 5 = 7$, and its corners divide each side of that $7 \times 7$ square into $2$ and $5$. This can be done in exactly two ways ($2$ then $5$, or $5$ then $2$, going round). Hence each $7 \times 7$ square contains exactly $2$ squares of side $\sqrt{29}$, and there are $2 \times 9 = 18$ of them — twice the number of $7 \times 7$ squares. ∎

solutions.title: Why no other placements
solutions.body: A square with corners on lattice points and side $\sqrt{29}$ has a side vector $(a, b)$ of integers with $a^2 + b^2 = 29$, so $\{|a|, |b|\} = \{2, 5\}$ (the upright option would need $29$ to be a perfect square). Then the square spans $|a| + |b| = 7$ in each direction, so it is inscribed in a unique $7 \times 7$ upright square, and the two orientations $(2, 5)$ and $(5, 2)$ give the two squares per $7 \times 7$ square. ∎

answer: There are $(10-k)^2$ upright $k\times k$ squares, and each contains exactly $k$ squares inscribed with corners on its sides (split each side as $j$ and $k-j$, $j = 0, \dots, k-1$).

solutions.title: Group squares by bounding square
solutions.body:
Every square with corners on the dots fits snugly in a smallest upright square (sides along grid lines) whose sides each contain one of its corners.

- **How many upright $k \times k$ squares?** The left side can be in $10 - k$ positions and the bottom in $10 - k$ positions, so $(10 - k)^2$.
- **How many squares does each one hold?** Go around a $k \times k$ upright square and put a corner at distance $j$ from each vertex ($j = 0, 1, \dots, k - 1$); $j = 0$ is the upright square itself and $j \ge 1$ gives a tilted square of side $\sqrt{j^2 + (k - j)^2}$. Distinct $j$ give distinct squares, so there are $k$ of them.

Different bounding squares give different squares, so the total is
$$\sum_{k=1}^{9} k (10 - k)^2 = 1(9^2) + 2(8^2) + \cdots + 9(1^2).$$
∎

solutions.title: Check on small grids

solutions.title: Count pipes per row

solutions.title: Formula for B

With $k$ rows of $10$ and $k - 1$ rows of $9$ (B starts and ends with a $10$-row): $10k + 9(k - 1) = 200$, so $19k = 209$, $k = 11$. Rows: $11 + 10 = 21$.

solutions.title: Pythagoras
solutions.body:
The top centre is above the midpoint of the two bottom centres, $5$ cm horizontally from each, and $10$ cm from each. Its height above them is $\sqrt{10^2 - 5^2} = \sqrt{75} = 5\sqrt3$. Add a radius at the bottom and top: $h = 10 + 5\sqrt3$ cm.

**Answer: $h = 10 + 5\sqrt3$ cm**

prompt:
Two identical rectangular crates are packed with cylindrical pipes, using different methods. Each pipe has diameter $10$ cm. A side view of the first four rows of each of the two different methods of packing is shown: in Crate A every row has $10$ pipes stacked directly on top of the row below; in Crate B the rows alternate between $10$ and $9$ pipes, each pipe resting in the gap between two pipes of the row below.

After the crates have been packed with $200$ pipes each, what is the difference in the total heights of the two packings? Explain your answer.

solutions.title: Compare the heights
solutions.body:
**Crate A:** $20$ rows stacked straight, height $20 \times 10 = 200$ cm.

**Crate B:** $21$ rows. Consecutive rows' centre lines are $5\sqrt3$ cm apart (part (b)), so the bottom and top centre lines are $20 \cdot 5\sqrt3 = 100\sqrt3$ cm apart. Add a radius below and above: $10 + 100\sqrt3 \approx 183.2$ cm.

Difference: $200 - (10 + 100\sqrt3) = 190 - 100\sqrt3 \approx 16.8$ cm, with Crate A higher.

**Answer: $190 - 100\sqrt3$ cm** (about $16.8$ cm)

solutions.title: Row by row
solutions.body:
Each extra row in A adds $10$ cm; each extra row in B adds only $5\sqrt3 \approx 8.66$ cm. A: $10 + 19 \cdot 10 = 200$. B: $10 + 20 \cdot 5\sqrt3$. Difference $190 - 100\sqrt3 \approx 16.8$ cm.

**Answer: $190 - 100\sqrt3$ cm**

prompt:
The volume of a sphere with radius $r$ is $\frac43 \pi r^3$. The *total* surface area of a cone with height $h$, slant height $s$, and radius $r$ is $\pi r^2 + \pi r s$.

A cylinder has a height of $10$ and a radius of $3$. Determine the *total* surface area, including the two ends, of the cylinder, and also determine the volume of the cylinder.

solutions.title: Ends plus unrolled side
solutions.body:
Two ends: $2\pi(3^2) = 18\pi$. The curved side unrolls into a rectangle $10$ high and $2\pi(3) = 6\pi$ wide: area $60\pi$. Total surface area: $78\pi$.

Volume: $\pi r^2 h = \pi(9)(10) = 90\pi$.

**Answer: surface area $78\pi$, volume $90\pi$**

solutions.title: Formula
solutions.body:
Total surface area $= 2\pi r(r + h) = 2\pi(3)(13) = 78\pi$; volume $= \pi r^2 h = 90\pi$.

**Answer: surface area $78\pi$, volume $90\pi$**

prompt:
The volume of a sphere with radius $r$ is $\frac43 \pi r^3$. The *total* surface area of a cone with height $h$, slant height $s$, and radius $r$ is $\pi r^2 + \pi r s$.

A cone, a cylinder and a sphere all have radius $r$. The height of the cylinder is $H$ and the height of the cone is $h$. The cylinder and the sphere have the same volume. The cone and the cylinder have the same total surface area. Prove that $h$ and $H$ cannot both be integers.
answer: Volumes give $H = \frac43 r$; surface areas give $s = r + 2H$; with $s = \sqrt{r^2 + h^2}$ this leads to $h^2 = 7H^2$, so $h = \sqrt7\,H$, and $\sqrt7$ is irrational.

solutions.title: Eliminate r and s
solutions.body:
**Volumes:** $\pi r^2 H = \frac43 \pi r^3$, so $H = \frac43 r$, i.e. $r = \frac34 H$.

**Surface areas:** $2\pi r^2 + 2\pi r H = \pi r^2 + \pi r s$. Dividing by $\pi r$: $2r + 2H = r + s$, so $s = r + 2H$.

**Cone:** the height, radius and slant height form a right triangle, so $s^2 = r^2 + h^2$.

Substituting $r = \frac34 H$ and $s = \frac34 H + 2H = \frac{11}{4} H$:
$$\frac{121}{16} H^2 = \frac{9}{16} H^2 + h^2 \implies h^2 = \frac{112}{16} H^2 = 7H^2.$$

So $h = \sqrt7\, H$. If $H$ and $h$ were both (positive) integers, $\sqrt7 = \frac{h}{H}$ would be rational — but $\sqrt7$ is irrational. ∎

solutions.title: Why √7 is irrational
solutions.body: Suppose $h^2 = 7H^2$ with positive integers $h, H$, and choose the solution with $H$ smallest. Then $7 \mid h^2$, and since $7$ is prime, $7 \mid h$; write $h = 7k$. Then $49k^2 = 7H^2$, so $H^2 = 7k^2$: the pair $(H, k)$ is another solution, with $k$ in the role of $H$. But $k = \frac{h}{7} < H$ (because $h^2 = 7H^2 < 49H^2$), contradicting the minimality of $H$. So no integer solution exists, and $h$, $H$ cannot both be integers. ∎

prompt:
A hat contains six slips of paper numbered from $1$ to $6$. Amelie and Bob each choose three slips from the hat without replacing any of the slips. Each of them adds up the numbers on his or her slips.

Determine the largest possible difference between Amelie's total and Bob's total. Explain how you found this difference.

solutions.title: Big three vs small three
solutions.body:
The difference is largest when one person has the three largest numbers and the other the three smallest: $4 + 5 + 6 = 15$ and $1 + 2 + 3 = 6$. Difference $9$.

**Answer: 9**

solutions.title: Using the total
solutions.body:
The totals add to $21$, so if one total is $T$ the difference is $|2T - 21|$. The largest possible $T$ is $15$ and the smallest $6$; either gives $|30 - 21| = |12 - 21| = 9$.

**Answer: 9**

prompt:
A hat contains six slips of paper numbered from $1$ to $6$. Amelie and Bob each choose three slips from the hat without replacing any of the slips. Each of them adds up the numbers on his or her slips.

List all possible groups of three slips that Amelie can choose so that her total is one more than Bob's total.

solutions.title: Her total must be 11
solutions.body:
The six numbers add to $21$, so Amelie's total $A$ and Bob's $B$ satisfy $A + B = 21$ and $A = B + 1$, giving $A = 11$.

Triples from $1$–$6$ with sum $11$: $\{1, 4, 6\}$, $\{2, 3, 6\}$, $\{2, 4, 5\}$. (With $6$: the other two sum to $5$: $1 + 4$, $2 + 3$. Without $6$ but with $5$: the other two sum to $6$ from $1$–$4$: $2 + 4$. Without $5$ or $6$: at most $2 + 3 + 4 = 9$.)

**Answer: $\{1,4,6\}$, $\{2,3,6\}$, $\{2,4,5\}$**

solutions.title: Check with Bob's slips
solutions.body: Bob gets the other three slips, which must total $10$. The complements of Amelie's groups are $\{2, 3, 5\}$, $\{1, 4, 5\}$ and $\{1, 3, 6\}$, each summing to $10$ ✓. Listing all triples with sum $10$ gives exactly these three, confirming the list.

prompt:
A hat contains six slips of paper numbered from $1$ to $6$. Amelie and Bob each choose three slips from the hat without replacing any of the slips. Each of them adds up the numbers on his or her slips.

Explain why it is impossible for Amelie and Bob to have the same total no matter which three slips each chooses.
answer: Their totals add to $1 + \cdots + 6 = 21$, which is odd, so they can't be equal.

solutions.title: Odd total
solutions.body: Every slip is taken, so the two totals add to $21$. Equal totals would add to an even number. $21$ is odd, so the totals are never equal. ∎

solutions.title: Half of 21
solutions.body: Equal totals would each be $21 \div 2 = 10.5$, not an integer. ∎

prompt:
A hat contains six slips of paper numbered from $1$ to $6$. Amelie and Bob each choose three slips from the hat without replacing any of the slips. Each of them adds up the numbers on his or her slips.

If more slips of paper are added to the hat, numbered consecutively from $7$ to $n$, what is the smallest value of $n > 6$ so that Amelie and Bob can each choose half of the slips numbered from $1$ to $n$ and obtain the same total? Explain why this value of $n$ works.

solutions.title: n must be even; try 8
solutions.body:
Each takes half the slips, so $n$ is even; $n = 7$ is impossible, so $n \ge 8$. For $n = 8$ the total is $36$, so each needs $18$: Amelie takes $1, 2, 7, 8$ and Bob takes $3, 4, 5, 6$. Both total $18$.

**Answer: $n = 8$**

solutions.title: Pairing trick
solutions.body:
For $n = 8$, pair the numbers as $(1, 8), (2, 7), (3, 6), (4, 5)$, each summing to $9$. Giving two pairs to each person gives equal totals $18$. And $n = 7$ fails because $7$ slips can't be split in half.

**Answer: $n = 8$**

prompt:
In the diagram, $AB$, $BC$, $CD$, $DE$, $EF$, $FG$, $GH$, and $HK$ all have length $4$, and all angles are right angles, with the exception of the angles at $D$ and $F$. (The figure is a rectangle $ABHK$ with $C$ and $G$ on $BH$; $CD$ and $GF$ rise vertically from $BH$, and $E$ lies between them below $DF$, with $\angle DEF = 90^\circ$.)

Determine the length of $DF$.

solutions.title: Pythagoras
solutions.body:
$\triangle DEF$ has a right angle at $E$ and legs $4, 4$: $DF^2 = 16 + 16 = 32$, $DF = 4\sqrt2$.

**Answer: $4\sqrt2$**

solutions.title: 45-45-90 triangle
solutions.body:
An isosceles right triangle's hypotenuse is $\sqrt2$ times a leg: $DF = 4\sqrt2$.

**Answer: $4\sqrt2$**

prompt:
In the diagram, $AB$, $BC$, $CD$, $DE$, $EF$, $FG$, $GH$, and $HK$ all have length $4$, and all angles are right angles, with the exception of the angles at $D$ and $F$. (The figure is a rectangle $ABHK$ with $C$ and $G$ on $BH$; $CD$ and $GF$ rise vertically from $BH$, and $E$ lies between them below $DF$, with $\angle DEF = 90^\circ$.)

If perpendicular $EM$ is drawn from $E$ to $DF$, what is the length of $EM$? Explain how you got your answer.

solutions.title: Area two ways
solutions.body:
Area of $\triangle DEF = \frac12 \cdot 4 \cdot 4 = 8$. Also area $= \frac12 \cdot DF \cdot EM = \frac12 \cdot 4\sqrt2 \cdot EM$. So $EM = \frac{16}{4\sqrt2} = 2\sqrt2$.

**Answer: $2\sqrt2$**

solutions.title: Half the hypotenuse
solutions.body:
$M$ is the midpoint of $DF$ (the triangle is isosceles), so $DM = 2\sqrt2$, and $\triangle DME$ is a $45$-$45$-$90$ triangle, giving $EM = DM = 2\sqrt2$.

**Answer: $2\sqrt2$**

prompt:
In the diagram, $AB$, $BC$, $CD$, $DE$, $EF$, $FG$, $GH$, and $HK$ all have length $4$, and all angles are right angles, with the exception of the angles at $D$ and $F$. (The figure is a rectangle $ABHK$ with $C$ and $G$ on $BH$; $CD$ and $GF$ rise vertically from $BH$, and $E$ lies between them below $DF$, with $\angle DEF = 90^\circ$.)

If perpendicular $EP$ is drawn from $E$ to $AK$, what is the length of $EP$? Explain how you got your answer.

solutions.title: Stack the distances
solutions.body:
$D$ and $F$ are both $4$ above line $BH$ (since $CD = GF = 4$), and $DF$ is horizontal; $AK$ is $4$ below $BH$. $E$ is $EM = 2\sqrt2$ below $DF$, so it is $4 - 2\sqrt2$ above $BH$, and
$$EP = 4 + (4 - 2\sqrt2) = 8 - 2\sqrt2.$$

**Answer: $8 - 2\sqrt2$** (about $5.17$)

solutions.title: Coordinates
solutions.body:
Put $A = (0, 0)$, so $B = (0, 4)$, $C = (4, 4)$, $D = (4, 8)$, and $F = (4 + 4\sqrt2, 8)$. $E$ is below the midpoint of $DF$ at depth $2\sqrt2$: $E = (4 + 2\sqrt2,\ 8 - 2\sqrt2)$. $AK$ is the $x$-axis, so $EP = 8 - 2\sqrt2$.

**Answer: $8 - 2\sqrt2$**

prompt:
In the diagram, $AB$, $BC$, $CD$, $DE$, $EF$, $FG$, $GH$, and $HK$ all have length $4$, and all angles are right angles, with the exception of the angles at $D$ and $F$. (The figure is a rectangle $ABHK$ with $C$ and $G$ on $BH$; $CD$ and $GF$ rise vertically from $BH$, and $E$ lies between them below $DF$, with $\angle DEF = 90^\circ$.)

What is the area of figure $ABCDEFGHK$? Explain how you got your answer.

solutions.title: Two rectangles minus a triangle
solutions.body:
Join $DF$ and $CG$. The figure is rectangle $ABHK$ plus rectangle $CGFD$ minus $\triangle DEF$.

- $CG = DF = 4\sqrt2$, so $BH = 4 + 4\sqrt2 + 4 = 8 + 4\sqrt2$; area of $ABHK = 4(8 + 4\sqrt2) = 32 + 16\sqrt2$.
- $CGFD$: $4 \times 4\sqrt2 = 16\sqrt2$.
- $\triangle DEF$: $8$.

Area $= 32 + 16\sqrt2 + 16\sqrt2 - 8 = 24 + 32\sqrt2$.

**Answer: $24 + 32\sqrt2$** (about $69.25$)

solutions.title: Shoelace with coordinates
solutions.body:
With $A(0,0)$, $B(0,4)$, $C(4,4)$, $D(4,8)$, $E(4+2\sqrt2, 8-2\sqrt2)$, $F(4+4\sqrt2, 8)$, $G(4+4\sqrt2, 4)$, $H(8+4\sqrt2, 4)$, $K(8+4\sqrt2, 0)$: the region below $y = 4$ is $4(8 + 4\sqrt2)$, and above it is the $4\sqrt2 \times 4$ rectangle with the triangle $DEF$ (area $8$) removed. Total $32 + 16\sqrt2 + 16\sqrt2 - 8 = 24 + 32\sqrt2$.

**Answer: $24 + 32\sqrt2$**

prompt:
In the diagram, a line is drawn through the points $A(0, 16)$ and $B(8, 0)$. Point $P$ is chosen in the first quadrant on the line through $A$ and $B$. Points $C$ and $D$ are then chosen on the $x$-axis and $y$-axis, respectively, so that $PDOC$ is a rectangle.

Determine the equation of the line through $A$ and $B$.

solutions.title: Slope and intercept
solutions.body:
Slope $= \frac{16 - 0}{0 - 8} = -2$, and the $y$-intercept is $16$ (point $A$). So $y = -2x + 16$.

**Answer: $y = -2x + 16$**

solutions.title: Intercept form
solutions.body:
A line with $x$-intercept $8$ and $y$-intercept $16$ is $\frac{x}{8} + \frac{y}{16} = 1$, i.e. $2x + y = 16$.

**Answer: $y = -2x + 16$**

prompt:
In the diagram, a line is drawn through the points $A(0, 16)$ and $B(8, 0)$. Point $P$ is chosen in the first quadrant on the line through $A$ and $B$. Points $C$ and $D$ are then chosen on the $x$-axis and $y$-axis, respectively, so that $PDOC$ is a rectangle.

Determine the coordinates of the point $P$ so that $PDOC$ is a square.

solutions.title: Equal sides
solutions.body:
Let $P = (c, -2c + 16)$. Then $PD = c$ (distance to the $y$-axis) and $PC = -2c + 16$ (distance to the $x$-axis). A square needs $c = -2c + 16$, so $c = \frac{16}{3}$ and $P = \left(\frac{16}3, \frac{16}3\right)$.

**Answer: $\left(\frac{16}{3}, \frac{16}{3}\right)$**

solutions.title: Intersect with y = x
solutions.body:
For a square, $P$ lies on $y = x$. Solving $x = -2x + 16$ gives $x = \frac{16}{3}$.

**Answer: $\left(\frac{16}{3}, \frac{16}{3}\right)$**

prompt:
In the diagram, a line is drawn through the points $A(0, 16)$ and $B(8, 0)$. Point $P$ is chosen in the first quadrant on the line through $A$ and $B$. Points $C$ and $D$ are then chosen on the $x$-axis and $y$-axis, respectively, so that $PDOC$ is a rectangle.

Determine the coordinates of all points $P$ that can be chosen so that the area of rectangle $PDOC$ is $30$.

solutions.title: Area equation
solutions.body:
With $P = (c, -2c + 16)$, the area is $c(-2c + 16) = 30$, i.e. $2c^2 - 16c + 30 = 0$, $c^2 - 8c + 15 = 0$, $(c - 3)(c - 5) = 0$. So $P = (3, 10)$ or $(5, 6)$; both are in the first quadrant and give area $30$.

**Answer: $(3, 10)$ and $(5, 6)$**

solutions.title: Hyperbola meets line
solutions.body:
Area $30$ means $xy = 30$. With $y = 16 - 2x$: $x(16 - 2x) = 30$, the same quadratic, $x = 3$ or $5$. Check: $3 \cdot 10 = 30$ ✓, $5 \cdot 6 = 30$ ✓.

**Answer: $(3, 10)$ and $(5, 6)$**

prompt: When the number $14$ has its digits reversed to form the number $41$, it is increased by $27$. Determine all $2$-digit numbers which are increased by $27$ when their digits are reversed.

solutions.title: Algebra
solutions.body:
For $\underline{a}\,\underline{b} = 10a + b$, reversing gives $10b + a$, an increase of $9(b - a)$. We need $9(b - a) = 27$, so $b = a + 3$ with $a \ge 1$, $b \le 9$: $14, 25, 36, 47, 58, 69$.

**Answer: 14, 25, 36, 47, 58, 69**

solutions.title: Check
solutions.body: $41 - 14 = 52 - 25 = 63 - 36 = 74 - 47 = 85 - 58 = 96 - 69 = 27$ ✓. Any other pair of digits differs by something other than $3$, giving a change other than $27$.

prompt:
Choose any three-digit integer $\underline{a}\,\underline{b}\,\underline{c}$ whose digits are all different. (When an integer is written in terms of its digits as $\underline{a}\,\underline{b}\,\underline{c}$, it means the integer is $100a + 10b + c$.)

Reverse the order of the digits to get a new three-digit integer $\underline{c}\,\underline{b}\,\underline{a}$. Subtract the smaller of these integers from the larger to obtain a three-digit integer $\underline{r}\,\underline{s}\,\underline{t}$, where $r$ is allowed to be $0$. Reverse the order of the digits of this integer to get the integer $\underline{t}\,\underline{s}\,\underline{r}$. Prove that, no matter what three-digit integer $\underline{a}\,\underline{b}\,\underline{c}$ you start with, $\underline{r}\,\underline{s}\,\underline{t} + \underline{t}\,\underline{s}\,\underline{r} = 1089$.
answer: The difference is $99k$ with $k = |a - c| \in \{1, \dots, 9\}$, whose digits are $k - 1,\ 9,\ 10 - k$; reversing and adding gives $100 \cdot 9 + 10 \cdot 18 + 9 = 1089$.

solutions.title: The difference is 99k
solutions.body:
Assume $a > c$ (otherwise swap roles). Then
$$\underline{r}\,\underline{s}\,\underline{t} = (100a + 10b + c) - (100c + 10b + a) = 99(a - c) = 99k,$$
with $k = a - c \in \{1, \dots, 9\}$. Since $99k = 100(k - 1) + 90 + (10 - k)$, its digits are $r = k - 1$, $s = 9$, $t = 10 - k$ (all between $0$ and $9$). Then
$$\underline{r}\,\underline{s}\,\underline{t} + \underline{t}\,\underline{s}\,\underline{r} = 100(r + t) + 20s + (t + r) = 100 \cdot 9 + 180 + 9 = 1089.$$
∎

solutions.title: Check all nine cases
solutions.body: The possible differences are $099, 198, 297, 396, 495, 594, 693, 792, 891$, and their reverses are $990, 891, 792, 693, 594, 495, 396, 297, 198$. Each pair adds to $1089$. ∎

prompt: Suppose that $N = \underline{a}\,\underline{b}\,\underline{c}\,\underline{d}$ is a four-digit integer with $a \le b \le c \le d$. When the order of the digits of $N$ is reversed to form the integer $M$, $N$ is increased by $P$. (Again, the first digit of $P$ is allowed to be $0$.) When the order of the digits of $P$ is reversed, an integer $Q$ is formed. Determine, with justification, all possible values of $P + Q$.

Jim shops at a strange fruit store. Instead of putting prices on each item, the mathematical store owner will answer questions about combinations of items.

(a) In Aisle 1, Jim receives the following answers to his questions:

| Jim's Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| What is the sum of the prices of an Apple and a Cherry? | 62 cents |
| What is the sum of the prices of a Banana and a Cherry? | 66 cents |

What is the difference between the prices of an Apple and a Banana? Which has a higher price? Explain how you obtained your answer.
answer: The difference is 4 cents; the Banana costs more.

solutions.title: Compare the two sums
solutions.body:
Both combinations contain one Cherry. Swapping the Apple for a Banana raises the total from 62 to 66 cents, so a Banana costs $66 - 62 = 4$ cents more than an Apple.

**Answer: 4 cents; the Banana has the higher price.**

solutions.title: Subtract equations
solutions.body:
Let the prices (in cents) be $A$, $B$, $C$. Then $A + C = 62$ and $B + C = 66$. Subtracting, $B - A = 4$.

**Answer: 4 cents; the Banana has the higher price.**

prompt:
Jim shops at a strange fruit store. Instead of putting prices on each item, the mathematical store owner will answer questions about combinations of items.

(b) In Aisle 2, Jim receives the following answers to his questions:

| Jim's Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| What is the sum of the prices of a Mango and a Nectarine? | 60 cents |
| What is the sum of the prices of a Pear and a Nectarine? | 60 cents |
| What is the sum of the prices of a Mango and a Pear? | 68 cents |

What is the price of a Pear? Explain how you obtained your answer.

solutions.title: Mango and Pear cost the same
solutions.body:
Let the prices be $M$, $N$, $P$ cents. From $M + N = 60$ and $P + N = 60$, we get $M = P$. Then $M + P = 68$ becomes $2P = 68$, so $P = 34$.

**Answer: 34 cents**

solutions.title: Add all three
solutions.body:
Adding the three equations: $2(M + N + P) = 188$, so $M + N + P = 94$. Since $M + N = 60$, $P = 94 - 60 = 34$.

**Answer: 34 cents**

prompt:
Jim shops at a strange fruit store. Instead of putting prices on each item, the mathematical store owner will answer questions about combinations of items.

(c) In Aisle 3, Jim receives the following answers to his questions:

| Jim's Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| What is the sum of the prices of a Tangerine and a Lemon? | 60 cents |
| How much more does a Tangerine cost than a Grapefruit? | 6 cents |
| What is the sum of the prices of a Grapefruit, a Tangerine and a Lemon? | 94 cents |

What is the price of a Lemon? Explain how you obtained your answer.

solutions.title: Find the Grapefruit first
solutions.body:
Let the prices be $T$, $L$, $G$ cents: $T + L = 60$, $T - G = 6$, $G + T + L = 94$.

From the first and third, $G = 94 - 60 = 34$. Then $T = 34 + 6 = 40$ and $L = 60 - 40 = 20$.

**Answer: 20 cents**

solutions.title: Eliminate T
solutions.body:
From $T = G + 6$: the third equation becomes $2G + 6 + L = 94$, i.e. $2G + L = 88$, and the first becomes $G + 6 + L = 60$, i.e. $G + L = 54$. Subtracting, $G = 34$, so $L = 54 - 34 = 20$.

**Answer: 20 cents**

prompt: (a) In the diagram, what is the perimeter of the sector of the circle with radius 12? Explain how you obtained your answer.

solutions.title: Two radii plus an arc
solutions.body:
The sector angle is $60^\circ$, which is $\frac{60}{360} = \frac16$ of a full circle. So the arc $AB$ has length $\frac16 \cdot 2\pi(12) = 4\pi$.

The perimeter is $OA + OB + \text{arc } AB = 12 + 12 + 4\pi = 24 + 4\pi \approx 36.6$.

**Answer: $24 + 4\pi$**

solutions.title: Arc length formula
solutions.body:
In radians, $60^\circ = \frac{\pi}{3}$, so the arc length is $r\theta = 12 \cdot \frac{\pi}{3} = 4\pi$. Perimeter: $24 + 4\pi$.

**Answer: $24 + 4\pi$**

prompt: (b) Two sectors of a circle of radius 12 are placed side by side, as shown. Determine the *area* of figure $ABCD$. Explain how you obtained your answer.

solutions.title: Two sixths of a circle
solutions.body:
Each $60^\circ$ sector is $\frac16$ of a circle of radius 12, so has area $\frac16 \cdot 144\pi = 24\pi$.

Figure $ABCD$ is two such sectors: $2 \cdot 24\pi = 48\pi \approx 150.8$.

**Answer: $48\pi$**

solutions.title: One third of a circle
solutions.body:
The two sectors together have the same area as a single sector of angle $120^\circ$, which is $\frac13$ of a circle: $\frac13 \cdot 144\pi = 48\pi$.

**Answer: $48\pi$**

prompt: (c) In the diagram, $AOB$ is a sector of a circle with $\angle AOB = 60^\circ$ and $OA = OB = 12$. $OY$ is drawn perpendicular to $AB$ and intersects $AB$ at $X$. What is the length of $XY$? Explain how you obtained your answer.

solutions.title: 30-60-90 triangle
solutions.body:
$OY$ is a radius, so $OY = 12$. Since $OA = OB$ and $\angle AOB = 60^\circ$, $\triangle OAB$ is equilateral, and $OX$ bisects $\angle AOB$, so $\angle AOX = 30^\circ$.

In the $30^\circ$-$60^\circ$-$90^\circ$ triangle $OAX$ with hypotenuse 12: $AX = 6$ and $OX = 6\sqrt3$.

So $XY = OY - OX = 12 - 6\sqrt3 \approx 1.61$.

**Answer: $12 - 6\sqrt3$**

solutions.title: Pythagoras
solutions.body:
$\triangle OAB$ is equilateral with side 12, and the perpendicular from $O$ bisects $AB$, so $AX = 6$. Then $OX = \sqrt{12^2 - 6^2} = \sqrt{108} = 6\sqrt3$, and $XY = 12 - 6\sqrt3$.

**Answer: $12 - 6\sqrt3$**

prompt: (d) Two sectors of a circle of radius 12 overlap as shown, with $P$ and $R$ the centres of the respective circles (each sector has a $60^\circ$ angle). Determine the area of the shaded region. Explain how you obtained your answer.

solutions.title: Sector minus triangle, twice
solutions.body:
By symmetry, $QS$ splits the shaded region into two equal parts. The right part is sector $PQS$ minus $\triangle PQS$.

- Sector $PQS$ has area $\frac16 \cdot 144\pi = 24\pi$.
- $\triangle PQS$ is equilateral with side 12 (as in part (c)); its height is $6\sqrt3$, so its area is $\frac12 \cdot 12 \cdot 6\sqrt3 = 36\sqrt3$.

So each part has area $24\pi - 36\sqrt3$, and the shaded region has area $48\pi - 72\sqrt3 \approx 26.1$.

**Answer: $48\pi - 72\sqrt3$**

solutions.title: Inclusion–exclusion
solutions.body:
The two sectors together make up the rhombus $PQRS$, with the shaded lens lying in both of them and every other point of the rhombus in exactly one. So area(sector $P$) + area(sector $R$) = area(rhombus $PQRS$) + area(shaded).

The rhombus is two equilateral triangles of side 12: area $2 \cdot 36\sqrt3 = 72\sqrt3$. So

$$\text{shaded} = 24\pi + 24\pi - 72\sqrt3 = 48\pi - 72\sqrt3.$$

**Answer: $48\pi - 72\sqrt3$**

prompt: (a) Each face of a 5 by 5 by 5 wooden cube is divided into 1 by 1 squares. Each square is painted black or white, as shown. Next, the cube is cut into 1 by 1 by 1 cubes. How many of these cubes have *at least* two painted faces? Explain how you obtained your answer.

solutions.title: Edges and corners
solutions.body:
A small cube has at least two painted faces exactly when it lies on an edge of the big cube (colours don't matter here).

- 8 corner cubes (three painted faces),
- each of the 12 edges has $5 - 2 = 3$ non-corner cubes (two painted faces).

Total: $8 + 12 \times 3 = 44$.

**Answer: 44**

solutions.title: Subtract the rest
solutions.body:
Of the $125$ small cubes, $3^3 = 27$ are inside (no paint), and each face has $3 \times 3 = 9$ cubes with exactly one painted face: $6 \times 9 = 54$. So $125 - 27 - 54 = 44$ cubes have at least two painted faces.

**Answer: 44**

Again, the cube is cut into 1 by 1 by 1 cubes.

(b) i. In terms of $k$, how many of these cubes have *exactly* two white faces? Explain how you obtained your answer.

solutions.title: Count along one edge
solutions.body:
A small cube with exactly two white faces lies on an edge but not at a corner (corner cubes have three faces, all white).

Along an edge there are $2k + 1$ cubes. Corners are white and the colours alternate along the edge, so the cubes in positions $1, 3, 5, \dots, 2k+1$ are white on both edge faces: that is $k + 1$ cubes, two of which are corners. (On an edge, the two visible squares of a cube have the same colour, since both are at the same position along the checkerboard pattern starting from a white corner.)

So each edge has $k + 1 - 2 = k - 1$ non-corner cubes with two white faces, and there are 12 edges:

$$12(k - 1) = 12k - 12.$$

Check with $k = 2$ (the 5-cube): each edge has positions 1–5, white at 1, 3, 5, so one non-corner cube per edge, 12 in total. ✓

**Answer: $12k - 12$**

prompt:

(b) ii. Prove that there is no value of $k$ for which the number of cubes having *at least* two white faces is 2006.
answer: The count is $12k - 12 + 8 = 12k - 4$, and $12k - 4 = 2006$ gives $k = 167.5$, not an integer.

solutions.title: Count, then solve
solutions.body:
Cubes with at least two white faces are those with exactly two white faces ($12k - 12$ of them, by part (i)) plus the 8 corner cubes (three white faces). Total: $12k - 4$.

If $12k - 4 = 2006$, then $12k = 2010$ and $k = 167.5$, which is not an integer. So no value of $k$ works. ∎

solutions.title: Divisibility
solutions.body: The total $12k - 4$ is always $\equiv 8 \pmod{12}$ (equivalently, it is a multiple of 4). But $2006 = 4 \cdot 501 + 2$ is not a multiple of 4. So the count can never be 2006. ∎

prompt:
(a) A class of 20 students was given a two question quiz. The results are listed below:

| Question number | Number of students who answered correctly |
|---|---|
| 1 | 18 |
| 2 | 14 |

Determine the smallest possible number and the largest possible number of students that could have answered both questions correctly. Explain why these are the smallest and largest possible numbers.

solutions.title: Count the wrong answers
solutions.body:
**Largest.** At most 14 students answered question 2 correctly, so at most 14 got both. This happens if all 14 are among the 18 who got question 1.

**Smallest.** 2 students missed question 1 and 6 missed question 2, so at most $2 + 6 = 8$ students missed at least one question. So at least $20 - 8 = 12$ got both right. This is achieved when the 2 and the 6 are different students: 12 got both, 6 got only question 1, 2 got only question 2.

**Answer: smallest 12, largest 14**

solutions.title: Inclusion–exclusion
solutions.body:
If $b$ students got both, then $18 + 14 - b$ got at least one, which is at most 20, so $b \ge 12$. And $b \le \min(18, 14) = 14$. Both extremes are achievable (as shown in Solution 1).

**Answer: smallest 12, largest 14**

prompt:
(b) A class of 20 students was given a three question quiz. The results are listed below:

| Question number | Number of students who answered correctly |
|---|---|
| 1 | 18 |
| 2 | 14 |
| 3 | 12 |

Determine the smallest possible number and the largest possible number of students that could have answered all three questions correctly. Explain why these are the smallest and largest possible numbers.

solutions.title: Count the wrong answers
solutions.body:
**Largest.** Only 12 answered question 3 correctly, so at most 12 got all three. This happens if those 12 also answered questions 1 and 2 correctly (possible since $12 \le 14 \le 18$).

**Smallest.** The numbers who missed questions 1, 2, 3 are 2, 6 and 8. So at most $2 + 6 + 8 = 16$ students missed at least one question, and at least $20 - 16 = 4$ got all three right.

This is achievable: 4 students get everything right, 2 miss only question 1, 6 miss only question 2, 8 miss only question 3. Check: question 1 correct $= 4 + 6 + 8 = 18$, question 2 correct $= 4 + 2 + 8 = 14$, question 3 correct $= 4 + 2 + 6 = 12$. ✓

**Answer: smallest 4, largest 12**

prompt:
(c) A class of 20 students was given a three question quiz. The results are listed below:

| Question number | Number of students who answered correctly |
|---|---|
| 1 | $x$ |
| 2 | $y$ |
| 3 | $z$ |

where $x \ge y \ge z$ and $x + y + z \ge 40$. Determine the smallest possible number of students who could have answered all three questions correctly in terms of $x$, $y$ and $z$.

solutions.title: Same idea as (b)
solutions.body:
The numbers who missed questions 1, 2, 3 are $20 - x$, $20 - y$, $20 - z$. So at most $(20 - x) + (20 - y) + (20 - z) = 60 - x - y - z$ students missed at least one question (this is between 0 and 20 since $40 \le x + y + z \le 60$). Therefore at least

$$20 - (60 - x - y - z) = x + y + z - 40$$

students answered all three correctly.

This is achievable: let $x + y + z - 40$ students answer everything correctly, $20 - x$ miss only question 1, $20 - y$ miss only question 2 and $20 - z$ miss only question 3. These add to 20 students, and e.g. question 1 is answered correctly by $20 - (20 - x) = x$ students. ✓

**Answer: $x + y + z - 40$**

- On each of his turns, Paul must remove from the list all of the positive divisors of the number that Carolyn has just removed.

For example, if $n = 6$, a possible sequence of moves is shown in this chart:

| Player | Number(s) removed | Number(s) remaining | Notes |

| Paul | 1, 2 | 3, 5, 6 | |
| Carolyn | 6 | 3, 5 | She could not remove 3 or 5 |
| Paul | 3 | 5 | |
| Carolyn | None | 5 | Carolyn cannot remove any number |
| Paul | 5 | None | |

In this example, the sum of the numbers removed by Carolyn is $4 + 6 = 10$ and the sum of the numbers removed by Paul is $1 + 2 + 3 + 5 = 11$.

(a) Suppose that $n = 6$ and Carolyn removes the integer 2 on her first turn. Determine the sum of the numbers that Carolyn removes and the sum of the numbers that Paul removes.

solutions.title: Play it out

- Carolyn needs a number with another divisor still in the list: only 6 (divisor 3) works. Paul removes 3. List: 4, 5.
- Neither 4 nor 5 has another divisor left, so Carolyn is stuck and Paul removes 4 and 5.

Carolyn's sum: $2 + 6 = 8$. Paul's sum: $1 + 3 + 4 + 5 = 13$.

solutions.body:
**Upper bound.** Every time Carolyn removes a number, Paul removes at least one number on his next turn (the number she removed must have another divisor in the list). So Carolyn removes at most half of the 10 numbers, i.e. at most 5 numbers, and her sum is at most $6 + 7 + 8 + 9 + 10 = 40$.

| Carolyn | Paul | Remaining |
|---|---|---|
| 7 | 1 | 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10 |
| 9 | 3 | 2, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10 |
| 6 | 2 | 4, 5, 8, 10 |
| 8 | 4 | 5, 10 |
| 10 | 5 | — |

So her maximum final sum is 40.

(c) If $n = 14$, prove that Carolyn cannot remove 7 numbers.
answer: She could only remove 7 numbers if they were exactly 8–14 (Paul removes divisors, which are at most 7); but after Paul removes 1 on his first turn, one of the primes 11, 13 remains and can never be removed by Carolyn.

solutions.title: Which 7 numbers would they be?
solutions.body:
Suppose Carolyn removes 7 numbers. Paul removes at least one number after each of her moves, and there are only 14 numbers, so Paul removes exactly 7 numbers, and every number is removed by one of them.

Paul only removes proper divisors of numbers Carolyn has removed. A proper divisor of a number $\le 14$ is at most 7. So Paul never removes any of $8, 9, \dots, 14$; these 7 numbers must all be Carolyn's, and they are all of her numbers.

Whatever Carolyn removes first, Paul then removes 1 (it divides everything). At that point at least one of the primes 11 and 13 is still in the list (Carolyn removed only one number). Say it is 11. Its only divisors are 1 and 11, and 1 is gone, so 11 has no divisor other than itself left: Carolyn can never remove it. Contradiction. So Carolyn cannot remove 7 numbers. ∎

solutions.title: Same move along parallel sides
solutions.body:
In square $ABCD$, going from $D$ to $C$ is the same move as going from $A$ to $B$: 6 right and 3 down. So $C = (3 + 6, 3 - 3) = (9, 0)$ and $t = 9$.

**Answer: $t = 9$**

solutions.title: Parallel slopes
solutions.body:
$AB$ has slope $\frac{6 - 9}{12 - 6} = -\frac12$. $DC \parallel AB$, so $\frac{0 - 3}{t - 3} = -\frac12$, giving $t - 3 = 6$ and $t = 9$.

**Answer: $t = 9$**

solutions.title: Formula
solutions.body:
An equilateral triangle with side $s$ has area $\frac{\sqrt3}{4}s^2 = \frac{\sqrt3}{4} \cdot 4 = \sqrt3$.

**Answer: $\sqrt3$**

prompt: (b) Determine the area of a regular hexagon with side length 2.

solutions.title: Six equilateral triangles
solutions.body:
Joining the centre to the six vertices cuts the hexagon into 6 triangles. Six $60^\circ$ angles fill the $360^\circ$ around the centre, and the triangles' angles at the vertices give $60^\circ + 60^\circ = 120^\circ$, the interior angle of a regular hexagon; so the hexagon is exactly six equilateral triangles of side 2.

Area $= 6\sqrt3$.

**Answer: $6\sqrt3$**

solutions.title: Rectangle plus two triangles
solutions.body:
A regular hexagon of side 2 splits into a central rectangle $2 \times 2\sqrt3$ (the distance between opposite vertices across is $2\sqrt3$) and two isosceles triangles with base $2\sqrt3$ and height 1. Area $= 4\sqrt3 + 2 \cdot \frac12 (2\sqrt3)(1) = 6\sqrt3$.

**Answer: $6\sqrt3$**

prompt: (c) In the diagram, regular hexagon $ABCDEF$ has sides of length 2. Using $A$, $C$ and $E$ as centres, portions of circles with radius 1 are drawn outside the hexagon. Using $B$, $D$ and $F$ as centres, portions of circles with radius 1 are drawn inside the hexagon. These six circular arcs join together to form a curve. Determine the area of the shaded region enclosed by this curve.

solutions.title: Add and subtract sectors
solutions.body:
Each interior angle of the hexagon is $120^\circ$.

- At $B$, $D$, $F$ the unshaded sectors inside the hexagon have angle $120^\circ$: each is $\frac13$ of a unit circle, area $\frac{\pi}{3}$; total $\pi$.
- At $A$, $C$, $E$ the shaded sectors outside the hexagon have angle $360^\circ - 120^\circ = 240^\circ$: each $\frac23 \pi$; total $2\pi$.

Shaded area $= 6\sqrt3 - \pi + 2\pi = 6\sqrt3 + \pi \approx 13.53$.

**Answer: $6\sqrt3 + \pi$**

solutions.title: Move the bites
solutions.body:
Each $120^\circ$ bite removed at $B$, $D$, $F$ can be matched against $120^\circ$ of the $240^\circ$ bulge at $A$, $C$, $E$; what is left over is three extra $120^\circ$ sectors, i.e. one full unit circle in total: area $\pi$. So the shaded area is the hexagon plus $\pi$: $6\sqrt3 + \pi$.

**Answer: $6\sqrt3 + \pi$**

$$n = a(1!) + b(2!) + c(3!) + d(4!) + e(5!).$$

In addition, each of the following conditions is satisfied:

- $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$, and $e$ are integers

- $0 \le b \le 2$

- $0 \le d \le 4$
- $0 \le e \le 5$.

(c) Prove that all integers $n$, where $0 \le n \le N$, can be written in this form.
answer: Repeated division with remainder by $120, 24, 6, 2, 1$; since $n < 720$ and each remainder is less than the previous divisor, each quotient satisfies its bound.

solutions.title: Repeated division with remainder
Counting argument
solutions.body: There are $2 \cdot 3 \cdot 4 \cdot 5 \cdot 6 = 720$ choices of $(a, b, c, d, e)$, and each gives a value between 0 and 719. If two different choices gave the same value, look at the largest index $k$ where they differ, say the coefficients there differ by at least 1. Then the difference of the two values is at least $k! - \sum_{j<k} j \cdot j! = k! - (k! - 1) = 1 > 0$ in absolute value — a contradiction. So the 720 choices give 720 different values in $\{0, \dots, 719\}$, i.e. every value. ∎

$$n = a(1!) + b(2!) + c(3!) + d(4!) + e(5!).$$

In addition, each of the following conditions is satisfied:

- $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$, and $e$ are integers
- $0 \le a \le 1$
- $0 \le b \le 2$
- $0 \le c \le 3$
- $0 \le d \le 4$
- $0 \le e \le 5$.

(d) Determine the sum of all integers $n$ that can be written in this form with $c = 0$.

solutions.title: Split into two independent parts
solutions.body:
With $c = 0$: $n = (a + 2b) + 24(d + 5e)$.

- $n_1 = a + 2b$ takes each value $0, 1, \dots, 5$ exactly once.
- $n_2 = d + 5e$ takes each value $0, 1, \dots, 29$ exactly once.

So the numbers are $n_1 + 24 n_2$, one for each of the $6 \times 30 = 180$ pairs, all different. Their sum is

$$30(0 + 1 + \dots + 5) + 6 \cdot 24 (0 + 1 + \dots + 29) = 30 \cdot 15 + 144 \cdot 435 = 450 + 62640 = 63090.$$

**Answer: 63090**

solutions.title: Average times count
solutions.body:
There are $2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 \cdot 6 = 180$ choices of $(a, b, d, e)$. Each coefficient takes each of its values equally often, so the average of $n$ is $\frac12(1) + 1(2) + 2(24) + \frac52 (120) = 0.5 + 2 + 48 + 300 = 350.5$. (No two choices give the same $n$, by the uniqueness of the representation.) Sum $= 180 \times 350.5 = 63090$.

**Answer: 63090**

solutions.body:
$QA$ and $OB$ are both horizontal, so $QABO$ is a trapezoid with parallel sides $QA = 2$ and $OB = 12$ and height $QO = 12$. Area $= \frac12 (2 + 12)(12) = 84$.

**Answer: 84**

solutions.title: Rectangle plus triangle
solutions.body:
Let $T = (2, 0)$. Rectangle $QATO$ has area $2 \times 12 = 24$, and right triangle $ATB$ has area $\frac12 (10)(12) = 60$. Total $84$.

**Answer: 84**

prompt:
(a) Solve the system of equations algebraically for $(x, y)$:

$$\begin{aligned} x + y &= 42 \\ x - y &= 10 \end{aligned}$$

solutions.title: Elimination
solutions.body:
Adding the equations: $2x = 52$, so $x = 26$. Then $y = 42 - 26 = 16$.

**Answer: $(x, y) = (26, 16)$**

solutions.title: Substitution
solutions.body:
From the second equation $x = y + 10$. Then $2y + 10 = 42$, $y = 16$, $x = 26$.

**Answer: $(26, 16)$**

prompt:
(b) Suppose that $p$ is an even integer and that $q$ is an odd integer. Explain why the system of equations

$$\begin{aligned} x + y &= p \\ x - y &= q \end{aligned}$$

has no positive integer solutions $(x, y)$.
answer: Adding gives $2x = p + q$, but $p + q$ is odd while $2x$ is even.

solutions.title: Add the equations
solutions.body: Adding gives $2x = p + q$. Since $p$ is even and $q$ is odd, $p + q$ is odd. But $2x$ is even for every integer $x$. So there is no integer $x$, let alone a positive integer solution. ∎

solutions.title: Same parity
solutions.body: For integers $x, y$, the numbers $x + y$ and $x - y$ differ by $2y$, an even number, so they always have the same parity. But $p$ and $q$ have different parities. ∎

prompt: (c) Determine all pairs of positive integers $(x, y)$ that satisfy the equation $x^2 - y^2 = 420$.

solutions.title: Factor pairs of the same parity
solutions.body:
$(x + y)(x - y) = 420$ with $x + y > x - y > 0$ (both positive since $x + y > 0$ and the product is positive). By part (b), $x + y$ and $x - y$ must have the same parity; since $420$ is even, both must be even.

Since $420 = 4 \cdot 105$, write $x + y = 2m$, $x - y = 2n$ with $mn = 105$, $m > n$: $(m, n) = (105, 1), (35, 3), (21, 5), (15, 7)$. Then $x = m + n$, $y = m - n$:

| $x + y$ | $x - y$ | $x$ | $y$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 210 | 2 | 106 | 104 |
| 70 | 6 | 38 | 32 |
| 42 | 10 | 26 | 16 |
| 30 | 14 | 22 | 8 |

**Answer: $(106, 104), (38, 32), (26, 16), (22, 8)$**

prompt: (a) In $\triangle PQR$, point $T$ is on side $QR$ such that $QT = 6$ and $TR = 10$. Explain why the ratio of the area of $\triangle PQT$ to the area of $\triangle PTR$ is $3 : 5$.
answer: Both triangles have the same height $h$ from $P$ to $QR$, so their areas are in the ratio of their bases $6 : 10 = 3 : 5$.

solutions.title: Same height
solutions.body:
Let $h$ be the distance from $P$ to line $QR$. It is the height of both triangles. So

$$\frac{|\triangle PQT|}{|\triangle PTR|} = \frac{\frac12 \cdot 6 \cdot h}{\frac12 \cdot 10 \cdot h} = \frac{6}{10} = \frac35. \;∎$$

prompt: (b) In $\triangle ABC$, point $D$ is the midpoint of side $BC$. Point $E$ is on $AC$ such that $AE : EC = 1 : 2$. Point $F$ is on $AD$ such that $AF : FD = 3 : 1$. If the area of $\triangle DEF$ is 17, determine the area of $\triangle ABC$.

solutions.title: Work outwards with base ratios
solutions.body:
Use the fact from (a): triangles with the same apex and bases on one line have areas in the ratio of their bases. Write $|XYZ|$ for the area of $\triangle XYZ$.

- On $AD$ with apex $E$: $|AEF| : |DEF| = AF : FD = 3 : 1$, so $|AEF| = 51$ and $|AED| = 68$.
- On $AC$ with apex $D$: $|ECD| : |AED| = EC : AE = 2 : 1$, so $|ECD| = 136$ and $|ADC| = 204$.
- On $BC$ with apex $A$: $|ABD| = |ADC|$ since $BD = DC$, so $|ABC| = 408$.

**Answer: 408**

solutions.title: Fractions of the whole
solutions.body:
$|ADC| = \frac12 |ABC|$; $|AED| = \frac13 |ADC| = \frac16 |ABC|$; $|DEF| = \frac14 |AED| = \frac{1}{24}|ABC|$. So $|ABC| = 24 \times 17 = 408$.

**Answer: 408**

prompt: (c) In the diagram, points $X$, $Y$ and $Z$ are on the sides of $\triangle UVW$, as shown. Line segments $UY$, $VZ$ and $WX$ intersect at $P$. Point $Y$ is on $VW$ such that $VY : YW = 4 : 3$. If $\triangle PYW$ has an area of 30 and $\triangle PZW$ has an area of 35, determine the area of $\triangle UXP$.

solutions.title: Area ratios along each cevian
solutions.body:
Let $a = |PYV|$, $b = |PZU|$, $c = |UXP|$, $d = |XVP|$.

- $\frac{|PYV|}{|PYW|} = \frac{VY}{YW} = \frac43$, so $a = 40$.
- Along $UW$, triangles with apex $V$ and with apex $P$ have the same base ratio $WZ : ZU$:
  $\frac{|VZW|}{|VZU|} = \frac{|PZW|}{|PZU|}$, i.e. $\frac{35 + 30 + 40}{b + c + d} = \frac{35}{b}$, so $b + c + d = 3b$ and $c + d = 2b$.
- Along $VW$ with apex $U$: $\frac{|UVY|}{|UYW|} = \frac43$, i.e. $3(40 + c + d) = 4(30 + 35 + b)$. With $c + d = 2b$: $120 + 6b = 260 + 4b$, so $b = 70$ and $c + d = 140$.
- Along $UV$ with apexes $W$ and $P$: $\frac{|UXW|}{|XVW|} = \frac{|UXP|}{|XVP|}$, i.e. $\frac{35 + 70 + c}{30 + 40 + d} = \frac{c}{d}$, giving $105d = 70c$, $d = \frac23 c$.

Then $c + \frac23 c = 140$, so $c = 84$.

**Answer: 84**

solutions.title: Finish with Ceva's theorem
solutions.body:
As in Solution 1, $a = 40$, $b = 70$, so $\frac{WZ}{ZU} = \frac{|PZW|}{|PZU|} = \frac{35}{70} = \frac12$ and $c + d = 140$.

By Ceva's theorem for the concurrent cevians $UY$, $VZ$, $WX$:

$$\frac{UX}{XV} \cdot \frac{VY}{YW} \cdot \frac{WZ}{ZU} = 1 \implies \frac{UX}{XV} = \frac{3}{4} \cdot 2 = \frac32.$$

Triangles $UXP$ and $XVP$ share the apex $P$, so $c : d = 3 : 2$, and $c = \frac35 \cdot 140 = 84$.

**Answer: 84**

prompt:
Jackson gave the following rule to create sequences:

"If $x$ is a term in your sequence, then the next term in your sequence is $\dfrac{1}{1-x}$."

For example, Mary starts her sequence with the number 3. The second term of her sequence is $\dfrac{1}{1-3} = \dfrac{1}{-2} = -\dfrac12$. Her sequence is now $3, -\frac12$.
The third term of her sequence is $\dfrac{1}{1-(-\frac12)} = \dfrac{1}{\frac32} = \dfrac23$. Her sequence is now $3, -\frac12, \frac23$.
The fourth term of her sequence is $\dfrac{1}{1-\frac23} = \dfrac{1}{\frac13} = 3$. Her sequence is now $3, -\frac12, \frac23, 3$.

Fabien starts his sequence with the number 2, and continues using Jackson's rule until the sequence has 2011 terms.

(a) What is the second term of his sequence?

solutions.title: Check by going on
solutions.body:
If the second term is $-1$, the third is $\frac{1}{1-(-1)} = \frac12$ and the fourth is $\frac{1}{1-\frac12} = 2$, back to the start — consistent with the pattern seen in Mary's example (the rule repeats every three terms).

**Answer: $-1$**

solutions.title: Count complete cycles
solutions.body:
The fourth term equals the first, and each term depends only on the previous one, so the sequence repeats every three terms: $2, -1, \frac12, 2, -1, \frac12, \dots$

Since $2011 = 3 \times 670 + 1$, the first $2010$ terms are $670$ full cycles (each containing one $2$), and the 2011th term is $2$. So there are $670 + 1 = 671$ terms equal to $2$.

**Answer: 671**

solutions.title: Use positions
solutions.body:
The terms equal to $2$ are exactly those in positions $1, 4, 7, \dots$, i.e. positions $3k + 1$. We need $3k + 1 \le 2011$, i.e. $0 \le k \le 670$: that is $671$ values of $k$. (No other term equals $2$, since the other terms in each cycle are $-1$ and $\frac12$.)

**Answer: 671**

prompt:
Alia has a bucket of coins. Each coin has a zero on one side and an integer greater than 0 on the other side. She randomly draws three coins, tosses them and calculates a score by adding the three numbers that appear.

(a) On Monday, Alia draws coins with a 7, a 5 and a 10. When she tosses them, they show 7, 0 and 10 for a score of 17. What other scores could she obtain by tossing these same three coins?

solutions.title: Subsets
solutions.body: A score is the sum of a subset of $\{5, 7, 10\}$: the empty sum $0$; singles $5, 7, 10$; pairs $12, 15, 17$; all three $22$. All eight sums are different, so the other scores are $0, 5, 7, 10, 12, 15, 22$.

prompt:
Alia has a bucket of coins. Each coin has a zero on one side and an integer greater than 0 on the other side. She randomly draws three coins, tosses them and calculates a score by adding the three numbers that appear.

(b) On Tuesday, Alia draws three coins and tosses them three times, obtaining scores of 60, 110 and 130. On each of these tosses, exactly one of the coins shows a 0. Determine the maximum possible score that can be obtained by tossing these three coins.

solutions.title: Add the equations
solutions.body:
Let the numbers on the coins be $a, b, c$. The three scores are different, so a different coin shows $0$ each time; say
$$a + b = 60,\quad a + c = 110,\quad b + c = 130.$$
Adding: $2(a + b + c) = 300$, so $a + b + c = 150$. The maximum score (all three numbers showing) is $150$.

**Answer: 150**

prompt:
Alia has a bucket of coins. Each coin has a zero on one side and an integer greater than 0 on the other side. She randomly draws three coins, tosses them and calculates a score by adding the three numbers that appear.

(c) On Wednesday, Alia draws one coin with a 25, one with a 50, and a third coin. She tosses these three coins and obtains a score of 170. Determine all possible numbers, other than zero, that could be on the third coin.

solutions.title: Cases for the first two coins
solutions.body:
The first two coins contribute $0$, $25$, $50$ or $75$. The third coin must show the rest of the $170$ — and it cannot show $0$, since the first two give at most $75 < 170$. So the third coin's number is
$$170 - 0 = 170,\quad 170 - 25 = 145,\quad 170 - 50 = 120,\quad 170 - 75 = 95.$$

**Answer: 170, 145, 120 or 95**

solutions.title: Check each
solutions.body:
Each value is achievable: third coin $170$ with both others showing $0$; $145$ with $25$ showing; $120$ with $50$ showing; $95$ with both showing ($25 + 50 + 95 = 170$). No other value is possible since the first two coins can only total $0, 25, 50, 75$.

**Answer: 170, 145, 120, 95**

prompt:
In rectangle $ABCD$, $P$ is a point on $BC$ so that $\angle APD = 90^\circ$. $TS$ is perpendicular to $BC$ with $BP = PT$, as shown. $PD$ intersects $TS$ at $Q$. Point $R$ is on $CD$ such that $RA$ passes through $Q$. In $\triangle PQA$, $PA = 20$, $AQ = 25$ and $QP = 15$. (In the diagram, $AB = 16$.)

(a) Determine the lengths of $BP$ and $QT$.

solutions.title: Pythagorean Theorem twice
solutions.body:
$\triangle ABP$ is right-angled at $B$, so $BP^2 = AP^2 - AB^2 = 400 - 256 = 144$ and $BP = 12$.

Then $PT = BP = 12$, and $\triangle QTP$ is right-angled at $T$, so $QT^2 = QP^2 - PT^2 = 225 - 144 = 81$ and $QT = 9$.

**Answer: $BP = 12$, $QT = 9$**

solutions.title: Spot the triples
solutions.body:
$\triangle ABP$ has hypotenuse $20$ and leg $16$: it is a $3$-$4$-$5$ triangle scaled by $4$, so $BP = 12$. Then $\triangle QTP$ has hypotenuse $15$ and leg $PT = 12$: a $3$-$4$-$5$ triangle scaled by $3$, so $QT = 9$.

**Answer: $BP = 12$, $QT = 9$**

prompt:
In rectangle $ABCD$, $P$ is a point on $BC$ so that $\angle APD = 90^\circ$. $TS$ is perpendicular to $BC$ with $BP = PT$, as shown. $PD$ intersects $TS$ at $Q$. Point $R$ is on $CD$ such that $RA$ passes through $Q$. In $\triangle PQA$, $PA = 20$, $AQ = 25$ and $QP = 15$. (In the diagram, $AB = 16$.)

(b) Show that $\triangle PQT$ and $\triangle DQS$ are similar. That is, show that the corresponding angles in these two triangles are equal.
answer: Right angles at $T$ and $S$, and vertically opposite angles at $Q$; the third angles then agree.

solutions.title: Angle chase
solutions.body:
- $\angle PTQ = \angle DSQ = 90^\circ$, since $TS \perp BC$ and $BC \parallel AD$.
- $\angle PQT = \angle DQS$, since they are vertically opposite angles ($P, Q, D$ are collinear and $T, Q, S$ are collinear).
- The angles of each triangle add to $180^\circ$, so the remaining angles are equal too: $\angle QPT = \angle QDS$.

So the triangles are similar (AA). ∎

solutions.title: Parallel lines
solutions.body: $BC \parallel AD$, and $PD$ is a transversal, so the alternate angles $\angle TPQ$ and $\angle SDQ$ are equal. Also $\angle PTQ = \angle DSQ = 90^\circ$. Two pairs of equal angles give $\triangle PQT \sim \triangle DQS$. ∎

prompt:
In rectangle $ABCD$, $P$ is a point on $BC$ so that $\angle APD = 90^\circ$. $TS$ is perpendicular to $BC$ with $BP = PT$, as shown. $PD$ intersects $TS$ at $Q$. Point $R$ is on $CD$ such that $RA$ passes through $Q$. In $\triangle PQA$, $PA = 20$, $AQ = 25$ and $QP = 15$. (In the diagram, $AB = 16$.)

(c) Determine the lengths of $QS$ and $SD$.

solutions.title: Use the similar triangles
solutions.body:
$ABTS$ is a rectangle, so $TS = AB = 16$ and $QS = 16 - QT = 16 - 9 = 7$.

From part (b), $\triangle PQT \sim \triangle DQS$, so $\dfrac{SD}{TP} = \dfrac{QS}{QT}$, i.e. $\dfrac{SD}{12} = \dfrac79$, and $SD = \dfrac{84}{9} = \dfrac{28}{3}$.

**Answer: $QS = 7$, $SD = \frac{28}{3}$**

solutions.title: Coordinates
solutions.body:
Put $A = (0,0)$, $D$ on the positive $x$-axis, $B = (0, 16)$. Then $P = (12, 16)$, $T = (24, 16)$, $S = (24, 0)$ and $Q = (24, 7)$ (since $QT = 9$), so $QS = 7$.

Line $PQ$ has slope $\frac{7 - 16}{24 - 12} = -\frac34$; it meets $y = 0$ when $x = 24 + 7 \cdot \frac43 = \frac{100}{3}$. So $D = (\frac{100}{3}, 0)$ and $SD = \frac{100}{3} - 24 = \frac{28}{3}$.

**Answer: $QS = 7$, $SD = \frac{28}{3}$**

prompt:
In rectangle $ABCD$, $P$ is a point on $BC$ so that $\angle APD = 90^\circ$. $TS$ is perpendicular to $BC$ with $BP = PT$, as shown. $PD$ intersects $TS$ at $Q$. Point $R$ is on $CD$ such that $RA$ passes through $Q$. In $\triangle PQA$, $PA = 20$, $AQ = 25$ and $QP = 15$. (In the diagram, $AB = 16$.)

(d) Show that $QR = RD$.
answer: $\triangle RQD$ is isosceles: $\angle RQD = \angle PQA = \angle TQP = \angle RDQ$ (or compute $QR = RD = \frac{175}{18}$).

solutions.title: Compute both lengths
solutions.body:
$\triangle QAS \sim \triangle RAD$ (common angle at $A$, right angles at $S$ and $D$). We have $AS = BT = 24$ and $DA = 24 + \frac{28}{3} = \frac{100}{3}$. Then
$$RD = QS \cdot \frac{DA}{SA} = 7 \cdot \frac{100/3}{24} = \frac{175}{18},\qquad RA = QA \cdot \frac{RD}{QS} = 25 \cdot \frac{175/18}{7} = \frac{625}{18}.$$
So $QR = RA - QA = \frac{625}{18} - \frac{450}{18} = \frac{175}{18} = RD$. ∎

solutions.title: Isosceles triangle by angles
solutions.body:
$\triangle PQA$ (sides $20, 15, 25$) and $\triangle TQP$ (sides $12, 9, 15$) have proportional sides: $\frac{20}{12} = \frac{15}{9} = \frac{25}{15} = \frac53$, so they are similar and $\angle PQA = \angle TQP$; call it $\alpha$.

$\angle RQD = \angle PQA = \alpha$ (vertically opposite). Since $CD \parallel TS$, the alternate angles give $\angle RDQ = \angle TQP = \alpha$.

So $\triangle RQD$ has two equal angles at $Q$ and $D$, hence $QR = RD$. ∎

prompt:
For a positive integer $n$, the $n$th triangular number is $T(n) = \dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}$.

For example, $T(3) = \dfrac{3(3+1)}{2} = \dfrac{3(4)}{2} = 6$, so the third triangular number is 6.

(a) There is one positive integer $a$ so that $T(4) + T(a) = T(10)$. Determine $a$.

solutions.title: List triangular numbers
solutions.body:
The triangular numbers are $1, 3, 6, 10, 15, 21, 28, 36, 45, 55, \dots$ We need $T(a) = 55 - 10 = 45 = T(9)$.

**Answer: 9**

prompt:
For a positive integer $n$, the $n$th triangular number is $T(n) = \dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}$.

For example, $T(3) = \dfrac{3(3+1)}{2} = \dfrac{3(4)}{2} = 6$, so the third triangular number is 6.

(b) Determine the smallest integer $b > 2011$ such that $T(b+1) - T(b) = T(x)$ for some positive integer $x$.

solutions.title: Simplify the difference
solutions.body:
$$T(b+1) - T(b) = \frac{(b+1)(b+2) - b(b+1)}{2} = \frac{2(b+1)}{2} = b + 1.$$
So $b + 1$ must be a triangular number greater than $2012$. Since $T(62) = 1953$ and $T(63) = 2016$, the smallest choice is $b + 1 = 2016$, i.e. $b = 2015$.

**Answer: 2015**

solutions.title: Think of dots
solutions.body:
$T(b+1)$ is a triangle of dots with rows $1, 2, \dots, b+1$; removing $T(b)$ leaves the last row, $b + 1$ dots. So we need the first triangular number above $2012$. Since $T(n) \approx n^2/2$, try $n \approx \sqrt{4024} \approx 63$: $T(63) = \frac{63 \cdot 64}{2} = 2016$ and $T(62) = 1953$. So $b = 2015$.

**Answer: 2015**

prompt:
For a positive integer $n$, the $n$th triangular number is $T(n) = \dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}$.

For example, $T(3) = \dfrac{3(3+1)}{2} = \dfrac{3(4)}{2} = 6$, so the third triangular number is 6.

(c) If $T(c) + T(d) = T(e)$ and $c + d + e = T(28)$, then show that $cd = 407(c + d - 203)$.
answer: Substitute $e = 406 - (c+d)$ into $c(c+1) + d(d+1) = e(e+1)$ and simplify.

solutions.title: Substitute and expand
solutions.body:
$T(28) = 406$, so $e = 406 - s$ where $s = c + d$. The first equation, times $2$, is $c^2 + c + d^2 + d = e(e+1)$, i.e.
$$c^2 + d^2 + s = (406 - s)(407 - s) = 406 \cdot 407 - 813 s + s^2.$$
Since $s^2 = c^2 + 2cd + d^2$, the $c^2$ and $d^2$ cancel:
$$s = 406 \cdot 407 - 813 s + 2cd \implies 2cd = 814 s - 406 \cdot 407.$$
Dividing by $2$: $cd = 407 s - 203 \cdot 407 = 407(c + d - 203)$. ∎

prompt:
For a positive integer $n$, the $n$th triangular number is $T(n) = \dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}$.

For example, $T(3) = \dfrac{3(3+1)}{2} = \dfrac{3(4)}{2} = 6$, so the third triangular number is 6.

(d) Determine all triples $(c, d, e)$ of positive integers such that $T(c) + T(d) = T(e)$ and $c + d + e = T(28)$, where $c \le d \le e$.

solutions.title: Use the prime 37
solutions.body:
By part (c), $cd = 407(c + d - 203)$, and $407 = 11 \times 37$. So $37 \mid cd$, and since $37$ is prime, $37$ divides $c$ or $d$.

Since $c \le d \le e$ and $c + d + e = 406$, we have $2d \le d + e < 406$, so $c \le d \le 203$. The multiples of $37$ up to $203$ are $37, 74, 111, 148, 185$.

The equation is symmetric in $c$ and $d$, so let $m$ be the one divisible by $37$ and solve for the other, $k$: $km = 407(k + m - 203)$ gives $k = \dfrac{407(m - 203)}{m - 407}$.
- $m = 37$: $k = \frac{407 \cdot (-166)}{-370}$, not an integer.
- $m = 74$: $k = \frac{407 \cdot 129}{333}$, not an integer.
- $m = 111$: $k = \frac{407 \cdot 92}{296}$, not an integer.
- $m = 148$: $k = \frac{407 \cdot 55}{259}$, not an integer.
- $m = 185$: $k = \frac{407 \cdot 18}{222} = 33$.

So $\{c, d\} = \{33, 185\}$, giving $c = 33$, $d = 185$, $e = 406 - 218 = 188$. Check: $d \le e$ ✓, and $T(33) + T(185) = 561 + 17205 = 17766 = T(188)$ ✓.

**Answer: $(33, 185, 188)$**

solutions.title: Factor the equation
solutions.body:
Rewrite $cd - 407c - 407d = -407 \cdot 203$ as
$$(407 - c)(407 - d) = 407^2 - 407 \cdot 203 = 407 \cdot 204 = 2^2 \cdot 3 \cdot 11 \cdot 17 \cdot 37.$$
Let $u = 407 - c$ and $v = 407 - d$. From $c \ge 1$ we get $u \le 406$; from $d \le 203$ (shown as in the first approach) we get $v \ge 204$; and $c \le d$ gives $u \ge v$. So $v^2 \le uv = 83028$, i.e. $204 \le v \le 288$, and also $v = 83028/u \ge 83028/406 > 204$.

The divisors of $83028$ between $205$ and $288$: only $222 = 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 37$ (others such as $204$ and $374$ fall outside). Then $u = 374$, so $c = 33$, $d = 185$, $e = 406 - 33 - 185 = 188 \ge d$ ✓.

**Answer: $(33, 185, 188)$**

prompt:
Adam and Budan are playing a game of Bocce. Each wants their ball to land closest to the jack ball. The positions of Adam's ball, $A$, Budan's ball, $B$, and the jack ball, $J$, are shown in the diagram. (In the diagram, $JP = 15$, $PA = 20$, $AQ = 15$, $BQ = 39$, with right angles at $P$, at $A$ (between $BA$ and $AQ$) and at $J$ (between $BJ$ and $JA$).)

(a) What is the distance from A to J?

solutions.title: Pythagorean Theorem
solutions.body:
In right triangle $JPA$, $AJ^2 = 15^2 + 20^2 = 225 + 400 = 625$, so $AJ = 25$.

**Answer: 25**

solutions.title: Scaled 3-4-5 triangle
solutions.body:
The legs $15$ and $20$ are $5 \times 3$ and $5 \times 4$, so the hypotenuse is $5 \times 5 = 25$.

**Answer: 25**

prompt:
Adam and Budan are playing a game of Bocce. Each wants their ball to land closest to the jack ball. The positions of Adam's ball, $A$, Budan's ball, $B$, and the jack ball, $J$, are shown in the diagram. (In the diagram, $JP = 15$, $PA = 20$, $AQ = 15$, $BQ = 39$, with right angles at $P$, at $A$ (between $BA$ and $AQ$) and at $J$ (between $BJ$ and $JA$).)

(b) What is the distance from B to A?

solutions.title: Pythagorean Theorem
solutions.body:
In right triangle $BAQ$ (right angle at $A$), $BA^2 = 39^2 - 15^2 = 1521 - 225 = 1296$, so $BA = 36$.

**Answer: 36**

solutions.title: Scaled 5-12-13 triangle
solutions.body:
$15 = 3 \times 5$ and $39 = 3 \times 13$, so this is a $5$-$12$-$13$ triangle scaled by $3$: $BA = 3 \times 12 = 36$.

**Answer: 36**

prompt:
Adam and Budan are playing a game of Bocce. Each wants their ball to land closest to the jack ball. The positions of Adam's ball, $A$, Budan's ball, $B$, and the jack ball, $J$, are shown in the diagram. (In the diagram, $JP = 15$, $PA = 20$, $AQ = 15$, $BQ = 39$, with right angles at $P$, at $A$ (between $BA$ and $AQ$) and at $J$ (between $BJ$ and $JA$).)

(c) Determine whose ball is closer to the jack ball, Adam's or Budan's.

solutions.title: Compute BJ
solutions.body:
In right triangle $BJA$ (right angle at $J$), $BJ^2 = BA^2 - AJ^2 = 1296 - 625 = 671$, so $BJ = \sqrt{671} \approx 25.9$.

Adam's ball is $AJ = 25$ from the jack, Budan's is about $25.9$. **Adam's ball is closer.**

solutions.title: Compare squares
solutions.body:
It is enough to compare squared distances: $AJ^2 = 625$ and $BJ^2 = 1296 - 625 = 671$. Since $671 > 625$, $BJ > AJ$.

**Answer: Adam's ball is closer.**

prompt: (a) When the numbers 25, 5 and 29 are taken in pairs and averaged, what are the three averages?

solutions.title: Check with the total
solutions.body:
Each number appears in two pairs, so the three averages add to $\frac{2(25 + 5 + 29)}{2} = 59$. Indeed $15 + 17 + 27 = 59$. ✓

**Answer: 15, 17, 27**

prompt: (b) When the numbers 2, 6 and $n$ are taken in pairs and averaged, the averages are 11, 4 and 13. Determine the value of $n$.

solutions.title: Match the averages
solutions.body:
The average of $2$ and $6$ is $4$. The average of $6$ and $n$ is larger than the average of $2$ and $n$, so $\frac{6 + n}{2} = 13$, giving $n = 20$. Check: $\frac{2 + 20}{2} = 11$. ✓

**Answer: 20**

solutions.title: Sum of the averages
solutions.body:
The three averages add to $\frac{2(2 + 6 + n)}{2} = 8 + n$. Since $11 + 4 + 13 = 28$, we get $n = 20$.

**Answer: 20**

prompt: (c) There are three numbers $a$, $b$ and 2. Each number is added to the average of the other two numbers. The results are 14, 17 and 21. If $2 < a < b$, determine the values of $a$ and $b$.

solutions.title: Order the expressions
solutions.body:
The three results are $2 + \frac{a + b}{2}$, $a + \frac{2 + b}{2}$, $b + \frac{2 + a}{2}$.

Each equals $\frac{(a + b + 2) + x}{2}$ where $x$ is the number itself, so the results are in the same order as $2 < a < b$. Hence
$$2 + \frac{a + b}{2} = 14 \quad\text{and}\quad b + \frac{2 + a}{2} = 21,$$
i.e. $a + b = 24$ and $a + 2b = 40$. Subtracting, $b = 16$, so $a = 8$. Check: $8 + \frac{2 + 16}{2} = 17$. ✓

**Answer: $a = 8$, $b = 16$**

solutions.title: Use the total
solutions.body:
Let $T = a + b + 2$. A number $x$ plus the average of the other two is $x + \frac{T - x}{2} = \frac{T + x}{2}$. So the three numbers are $28 - T$, $34 - T$, $42 - T$, and they add to $T$:
$$104 - 3T = T \implies T = 26.$$
The numbers are $2, 8, 16$. With $2 < a < b$: $a = 8$, $b = 16$.

**Answer: $a = 8$, $b = 16$**

prompt:
The diagram shows one of the infinitely many lines that pass through the point $(2, 6)$.

(a) A line through the point $(2, 6)$ has slope $-3$. Determine the $x$- and $y$-intercepts of this line.

solutions.title: Find the equation
solutions.body:
The line is $y = -3x + c$. Since $(2, 6)$ is on it, $6 = -6 + c$, so $c = 12$: $y = -3x + 12$. The $y$-intercept is $12$; setting $y = 0$ gives $x = 4$.

**Answer: $x$-intercept $4$, $y$-intercept $12$**

solutions.title: Walk along the slope
solutions.body:
From $(2, 6)$, moving left $2$ to $x = 0$ raises $y$ by $3 \times 2 = 6$, giving $(0, 12)$. Moving right to reach $y = 0$ requires dropping $6$, i.e. moving right $6 / 3 = 2$, giving $(4, 0)$.

**Answer: $x$-intercept $4$, $y$-intercept $12$**

prompt:
The diagram shows one of the infinitely many lines that pass through the point $(2, 6)$.

(b) Another line through the point $(2, 6)$ has slope $m$. Determine the $x$- and $y$-intercepts of this line in terms of $m$.

solutions.title: General equation
solutions.body:
The line is $y = mx + c$ with $6 = 2m + c$, so $c = 6 - 2m$: the $y$-intercept is $6 - 2m$.

Setting $y = 0$: $mx = 2m - 6$, so $x = 2 - \frac6m$ (this needs $m \ne 0$; a horizontal line has no $x$-intercept).

**Answer: $x$-intercept $2 - \frac6m$, $y$-intercept $6 - 2m$**

solutions.title: Point-slope form
solutions.body:
$y - 6 = m(x - 2)$. At $x = 0$: $y = 6 - 2m$. At $y = 0$: $-6 = m(x - 2)$, so $x = 2 - \frac6m$ (for $m \ne 0$). Check with $m = -3$: intercepts $12$ and $4$, matching part (a).

**Answer: $x$-intercept $2 - \frac6m$, $y$-intercept $6 - 2m$**

prompt:
The diagram shows one of the infinitely many lines that pass through the point $(2, 6)$.

(c) A line through the point $(2, 6)$ has slope $m$, and crosses the positive $x$-axis at $P$ and the positive $y$-axis at $Q$, as shown. Determine the two values of $m$ for which $\triangle POQ$ has an area of 25.

solutions.title: Area in terms of m
solutions.body:
By part (b), $OP = 2 - \frac6m$ and $OQ = 6 - 2m$. The area condition is
$$\tfrac12\left(2 - \tfrac6m\right)(6 - 2m) = 25 \iff (2m - 6)(6 - 2m) = 50m \iff -4m^2 + 24m - 36 = 50m,$$
so $4m^2 + 26m + 36 = 0$, i.e. $2m^2 + 13m + 18 = 0$, $(2m + 9)(m + 2) = 0$.

So $m = -\frac92$ or $m = -2$. Both are negative, so both intercepts are positive ($m = -2$: $P = (5, 0)$, $Q = (0, 10)$; $m = -\frac92$: $P = (\frac{10}{3}, 0)$, $Q = (0, 15)$).

**Answer: $m = -2$ or $m = -\frac92$**

solutions.title: Use intercepts as unknowns
solutions.body:
Let $P = (p, 0)$, $Q = (0, q)$ with $p, q > 0$. The line is $\frac xp + \frac yq = 1$, and $(2, 6)$ lies on it: $\frac2p + \frac6q = 1$, i.e. $2q + 6p = pq$. The area gives $pq = 50$.

So $2q + 6p = 50$, $q = 25 - 3p$, and $p(25 - 3p) = 50$: $3p^2 - 25p + 50 = 0$, $(3p - 10)(p - 5) = 0$.

- $p = 5$, $q = 10$: slope $-\frac{q}{p} = -2$.
- $p = \frac{10}{3}$, $q = 15$: slope $-\frac{15}{10/3} = -\frac92$.

**Answer: $m = -2$ or $m = -\frac92$**

prompt:
(a) In Town A, five students are standing at different intersections on the same east-west street, as shown. The distances between adjacent intersections are given in kilometres: from west to east, Abe, Bo, Carla, Denise and Ernie, with Abe–Bo $1$ km, Bo–Carla $2$ km, Carla–Denise $4$ km and Denise–Ernie $7$ km.

The students agree to meet somewhere on the street such that the total distance travelled by all five students is as small as possible. Where should the students meet?

solutions.title: Pair up the outside students
solutions.body:
The meeting point should be between Abe and Ernie (otherwise moving it toward them shortens everyone's walk). Anywhere between them, Abe and Ernie together walk $1 + 2 + 4 + 7 = 14$ km.

Likewise, Bo and Denise together walk $2 + 4 = 6$ km anywhere between them, and more outside. That leaves Carla, whose distance is smallest ($0$) when they meet at her intersection.

**Answer: at Carla's intersection** (total $14 + 6 = 20$ km)

solutions.title: Compare totals
solutions.body:
Put Abe at $0$, so Bo is at $1$, Carla at $3$, Denise at $7$, Ernie at $14$.
- Meet at Bo: $1 + 0 + 2 + 6 + 13 = 22$.
- Meet at Carla: $3 + 2 + 0 + 4 + 11 = 20$.
- Meet at Denise: $7 + 6 + 4 + 0 + 7 = 24$.

Moving from Carla in either direction, three students get farther away and only two get closer, so the total increases. The minimum is at Carla.

**Answer: at Carla's intersection**

prompt: (b) In Town B, there is an even number of students. The students are standing at different intersections on a straight north-south street. The students agree to meet somewhere on the street that will make the total distance travelled as small as possible. With justification, determine all possible locations where the students could meet.
answer: Anywhere between the two middle students (the $n$th and $(n+1)$th of $2n$, counted from the north), inclusive.

solutions.title: Peel off pairs from the outside
solutions.body:
Number the $2n$ students $1, 2, \dots, 2n$ from north to south.

If the meeting point $P$ is north of student $1$ (or south of student $2n$), moving it to student $1$ (or $2n$) shortens everyone's walk. So $P$ lies between students $1$ and $2n$, where these two together always walk exactly the distance between them — a constant.

Repeat with students $2$ and $2n - 1$: if $P$ is outside the stretch between them, moving $P$ to the nearer of them shortens the walks of students $2, \dots, 2n-1$ and keeps the pair $1, 2n$ constant. So $P$ lies between them, where their combined distance is constant.

Continuing, $P$ must lie between students $n$ and $n + 1$, and at every such point each pair $(k, 2n + 1 - k)$ walks the constant distance between them. So the total is the same (and minimal) everywhere from student $n$ to student $n + 1$.

**Answer: anywhere between the two middle students, inclusive.**

solutions.title: How the total changes
solutions.body:
Move the meeting point a small distance $\delta$ south. Every student north of it walks $\delta$ farther, every student south of it walks $\delta$ less. So the total changes by $\delta \times (\#\text{north} - \#\text{south})$.

- If more students are south of the point, moving south lowers the total; if more are north, moving north lowers it.
- Strictly between the $n$th and $(n+1)$th students there are exactly $n$ north and $n$ south, so the total does not change at all there.

So the total decreases as we approach the middle stretch from either side and is constant on it: the minimum is achieved exactly on the segment from student $n$ to student $n + 1$ (inclusive).

**Answer: anywhere between the two middle students, inclusive.**

prompt:
(c) In Town C, the streets run north-south and east-west forming a positive $xy$-plane with intersections every 1 km apart, as shown. One hundred students are standing at different intersections. The first 50 students, numbered 1 to 50, stand so that the student numbered $k$ stands at intersection $(2^k, k)$. (For example, student 5 stands at $(32, 5)$.) The remaining students, numbered 51 to 100, stand so that the student numbered $j$ stands at intersection $(j - 50, 2j - 100)$.

The students can only travel along the streets, and they agree to meet at an intersection that will make the total distance travelled by all students as small as possible. With justification, determine all possible intersections at which the students could meet.

solutions.title: Minimize east-west and north-south separately
solutions.body:
Travelling along streets, a student at $(a, b)$ needs $|x - a| + |y - b|$ km to reach $(x, y)$. So the total distance is
$$\sum |x - a_i| \;+\; \sum |y - b_i|,$$
and we can minimize the two sums separately. By part (b), each sum (with $100$ values) is minimized exactly between the $50$th and $51$st values in sorted order.

**$x$-coordinates.** Students $1$–$50$: $2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, \dots, 2^{50}$. Students $51$–$100$: $1, 2, 3, \dots, 50$. Values below $45$: five powers ($2, 4, 8, 16, 32$) and $1, \dots, 44$ — that is $49$ values. The $50$th and $51$st are $45$ and $46$. So $x \in [45, 46]$: at an intersection, $x = 45$ or $46$.

**$y$-coordinates.** Students $1$–$50$: $1, 2, \dots, 50$. Students $51$–$100$: $2, 4, \dots, 100$. Values $\le 33$: $33 + 16 = 49$. The value $34$ appears twice (as $34$ in both lists), so the $50$th and $51$st are both $34$: $y = 34$.

**Answer: $(45, 34)$ or $(46, 34)$**

prompt: (a) Find an equation of the line that passes through the points $(2, 0)$ and $(0, 4)$.

solutions.title: Slope and intercept
solutions.body:
The slope is $\frac{4 - 0}{0 - 2} = -2$ and the line passes through $(0, 4)$, so its $y$-intercept is $4$: $y = -2x + 4$.

**Answer: $y = -2x + 4$**

solutions.title: Check both points
solutions.body:
Try $y = mx + b$: from $(0, 4)$, $b = 4$; from $(2, 0)$, $0 = 2m + 4$ so $m = -2$. Hence $y = -2x + 4$ (equivalently $2x + y = 4$).

**Answer: $y = -2x + 4$**

A cube with edge length 9 cm contains a certain amount of water. When the cube has one face resting on the ground, the depth of the water is 1 cm, as shown.

(b) The cube is turned so that one edge, $PQ$, is on the ground with the opposite edge, $MN$, directly above it. Calculate the depth of the water in the cube.

solutions.title: Triangular prism
solutions.body:
The volume is $81$ cm³ (part (a)). Now the water is a triangular prism of length $PQ = 9$ whose cross-section is a right isosceles triangle $APC$ with the right angle at $P$ (at the bottom). If the depth is $h$, the hypotenuse $AC$ (the water surface) has length $2h$ and the triangle's area is $\frac12 (2h)(h) = h^2$.

So $9h^2 = 81$, $h^2 = 9$ and $h = 3$ cm.

**Answer: 3 cm**

solutions.title: Use the legs
solutions.body:
The cross-section is a right isosceles triangle with legs $a$ along the two bottom faces. Its area is $\frac12 a^2$, so $9 \cdot \frac12 a^2 = 81$ gives $a^2 = 18$, $a = 3\sqrt2$. The depth is the altitude from the right angle to the hypotenuse, which is $\frac{a}{\sqrt2} = 3$ cm.

**Answer: 3 cm**

prompt:
A cube with edge length 9 cm contains a certain amount of water. When the cube has one face resting on the ground, the depth of the water is 1 cm, as shown.

(c) The cube is now positioned so that a single corner, $P$, is on the ground with the opposite corner, $N$, directly above it. To the nearest hundredth of a centimetre, calculate the depth of the water in the cube.

solutions.title: Tetrahedron volume two ways
solutions.body:
The water is a tetrahedron $PRST$ with $R, S, T$ on the three edges at $P$, and by symmetry $PR = PS = PT = y$. Its three faces at $P$ are right isosceles triangles, so its volume is $\frac13 \cdot \frac12 y^2 \cdot y = \frac{y^3}{6}$. Setting this equal to $81$: $y^3 = 486$, $y = \sqrt[3]{486} \approx 7.862$ (less than $9$, so it fits).

The top face $RST$ is equilateral with side $\sqrt2\,y$, so its area is $\frac{\sqrt3}{4}(2y^2) = \frac{\sqrt3}{2}y^2$. Using it as the base with height $h$ (the depth): $\frac13 \cdot \frac{\sqrt3}{2} y^2 h = \frac{y^3}{6}$, so
$$h = \frac{y}{\sqrt3} = \frac{\sqrt[3]{486}}{\sqrt3} \approx 4.539.$$

**Answer: 4.54 cm**

solutions.title: Coordinates
solutions.body:
Put $P$ at the origin with the three cube edges along the axes. The ground is perpendicular to the diagonal $PN$, i.e. to the direction $(1, 1, 1)$, so the height of a point $(x, y, z)$ above the ground is $\frac{x + y + z}{\sqrt3}$.

The water fills the region $x + y + z \le s$ (with $x, y, z \ge 0$), a tetrahedron with volume $\frac{s^3}{6}$. So $\frac{s^3}{6} = 81$, $s = \sqrt[3]{486} \approx 7.862$, and the depth is $\frac{s}{\sqrt3} \approx 4.539$ cm.

**Answer: 4.54 cm**

prompt:

(d) On a fourth flight, exactly \$142 was collected in baggage fees. Explain why there must be at least one passenger who checked at least three bags.
answer: $20a + 27b = 142$ has no solution in non-negative integers ($b = 0,\dots,5$ all fail), so someone checked $\ge 3$ bags.

solutions.title: Try all possibilities
solutions.body:
Suppose everyone checked at most two bags: $a$ passengers with one bag (\$20) and $b$ with two (\$27). Then $20a + 27b = 142$, so $a = \frac{142 - 27b}{20}$. Since $27b \le 142$, $b \le 5$:

| $b$ | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $a$ | 7.1 | 5.75 | 4.4 | 3.05 | 1.7 | 0.35 |

None is an integer, so this is impossible: someone checked at least three bags. (E.g. $4 \times 27 + 34 = 142$.)

solutions.title: Last digits
solutions.body: $20a$ always ends in $0$, so $27b$ must end in $2$ (as $142$ does). The multiples of $27$ ending in $2$ are $27 \times 6 = 162, 27 \times 16, \dots$ — the smallest is $162 > 142$. So no combination of one- and two-bag passengers gives \$142, and someone must have checked at least three bags.

solutions.body:
For $k \le 50$ the largest sum is $99$, so $k > 50$. With $k = 51$ there is one pair $(49, 51)$; each increase of $k$ adds one pair, $(100 - k, k)$. Ten pairs: $(49, 51), \dots, (40, 60)$, so $k = 60$.

**Answer: 60**

solutions.title: Count with a formula
solutions.body:
Pairs are $(a, 100 - a)$ with $a < 50$ and $100 - a \le k$, i.e. $100 - k \le a \le 49$. For $51 \le k \le 99$ that is $49 - (100 - k) + 1 = k - 50$ pairs. Setting $k - 50 = 10$ gives $k = 60$.

**Answer: 60**

prompt:
Cards in a deck are numbered consecutively with positive integers. The cards are selected in pairs, $(a, b)$ with $a < b$, to create a given sum, $a + b$. For example, Anna has a set of cards numbered from 1 to 50 and she is required to create a sum of 60. Two of the pairs that she can select are $(10, 50)$ and $(25, 35)$.

(d) Derrick has a set of 75 cards numbered consecutively from 1 to 75. He can select exactly 33 pairs that have a sum of $S$. Determine, with justification, all possible values of $S$.

solutions.title: Odd and even cases
solutions.body:
**$S = 2k + 1$ odd.** The pairs are $(a, S - a)$ for $a = 1, \dots, k$.
- If $2k \le 75$ all are allowed: $k$ pairs. $k = 33$ gives $S = 67$.
- If $2k > 75$, we also need $b = S - a \le 75$, i.e. $a \ge 2k - 74$: $k - (2k - 74) + 1 = 75 - k$ pairs. $75 - k = 33$ gives $k = 42$, $S = 85$.

**$S = 2k$ even.** The pairs are $(a, S - a)$ for $a = 1, \dots, k - 1$.
- If $2k - 1 \le 75$: $k - 1$ pairs, so $k = 34$, $S = 68$.
- If $2k - 1 > 75$: $a \ge 2k - 75$, giving $(k - 1) - (2k - 75) + 1 = 75 - k$ pairs, so $k = 42$, $S = 84$.

**Answer: $S = 67, 68, 84, 85$** (e.g. $S = 84$: $(9, 75), (10, 74), \dots, (41, 43)$)

solutions.title: Symmetry
solutions.body:
The map $(a, b) \mapsto (76 - b, 76 - a)$ turns a pair with sum $S$ into a pair with sum $152 - S$ (and keeps $1 \le a < b \le 75$). So the number of pairs $N(S)$ satisfies $N(S) = N(152 - S)$.

For $S \le 76$, every pair $(a, S - a)$ with $1 \le a < S/2$ is allowed (as $S - a \le 75$), so $N(S) = \lfloor (S - 1)/2 \rfloor$. This equals $33$ exactly for $S = 67, 68$.

For $S \ge 76$, use the symmetry: $N(S) = N(152 - S) = 33$ iff $152 - S \in \{67, 68\}$, i.e. $S = 85$ or $84$.

**Answer: $S = 67, 68, 84, 85$**

prompt: (a) A circle of radius 2 and a circle of radius 5 are externally tangent to each other at $T$ and tangent to a horizontal line at points $P$ and $Q$, as shown. If points $O$ and $C$ are the centres of the circles, then $O$, $T$, $C$ are collinear and both $OP$ and $CQ$ are perpendicular to $PQ$. By constructing a line segment passing through $O$ and parallel to $PQ$, determine the distance between $P$ and $Q$.

solutions.title: Right triangle with the centres
solutions.body:
Draw $OR \parallel PQ$ with $R$ on $CQ$. Then $ORQP$ is a rectangle, so $RQ = OP = 2$ and $CR = 5 - 2 = 3$. Also $OC = 2 + 5 = 7$. In right triangle $ORC$:
$$OR^2 = 7^2 - 3^2 = 40,$$
so $PQ = OR = \sqrt{40} = 2\sqrt{10}$.

**Answer: $2\sqrt{10}$**

solutions.title: General formula
solutions.body:
For tangent circles of radii $r$ and $R$ on a line, the same construction gives $PQ^2 = (R + r)^2 - (R - r)^2 = 4Rr$, so $PQ = 2\sqrt{Rr}$. Here $2\sqrt{2 \cdot 5} = 2\sqrt{10} \approx 6.32$.

**Answer: $2\sqrt{10}$**
